source.title: CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits
source.authors: Mehrshad Saadatinia; Parsa Razmara; Ardalan Aryashad; Ali Abbasi; Seyedarmin Azizi

record.tranche_reason: The study tests refusal steering with a multi-layer SAE circuit and compares it with single-layer contrastive activation addition, a difference-in-means method. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position projection ablation.
record.gate_note: The refusal results in Appendix E bear on refusal interventions: a decision-point SAE circuit is steered against refusal, and single-layer CAA is compared at several coefficients. The SAE circuit is not the claimed single difference-in-means direction. The study does not test adding the claimed direction on harmless requests. Other toxicity, emotion, and sycophancy results are not refusal results; capability results are reported for general steering rather than refusal steering.
record.test_reason: Appendix E reports refusal rates on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (AdvBench, N=100) under single-layer subtraction of a harmful-minus-benign DiffMean (CAA) vector at layer 20. That intervention bears weakly on V1. The study also argues explicitly that such an input-level DiffMean vector captures harmful content rather than the refusal mechanism. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position directional ablation. The headline 89%→0% result comes from the authors' own multi-layer SAE circuit, which is not the V1 direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report that decision-point multi-layer SAE-circuit steering drops refusal from 89% to 0% at λ=−3 with coherent output, while single-layer CAA at the same coefficient leaves refusal virtually intact. They attribute this to CAA's input-level DiffMean capturing content rather than the refusal decision. They also state that refusal is 'structurally shallow and highly localized', consistent with Arditi et al.
record.recipe_differences: The refusal intervention discovers a decision-point, multi-layer SAE feature circuit using same-content refusal/compliance contrasts and steers its synthesized vectors. It does not project out a single harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference direction at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: For the tested refusal intervention, CircuitSteer changes refusal rate with steering coefficient: 0% at λ = −3 and 78% at λ = −1. CAA results also vary by coefficient.

fits_no_version.finding: A multi-layer SAE feature circuit found at the first generated token, using same-harmful-prompt refusal/compliance contrasts, cuts refusal from 89% to 0% at λ=−3 (78% at λ=−1). The authors argue that input-level DiffMean captures harmful content rather than refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-specific features at the generation decision point, contrasted with harmful content held fixed, give stronger refusal control than an input-level harmful-minus-harmless vector.

record.problems: The refusal-rate evaluation uses 100 held-out prompts and keyword-based detection; no uncertainty estimate is reported for those refusal results. The CAA comparator is a single-layer steering intervention, not the claim's all-layer, all-position projection ablation. Capability results are reported for general steering, not for the refusal-specific intervention.
record.rows_left_out: Perplexity entries in Appendix E.2 are not listed as separate rows because the claim versions concern refusal behavior and general capability, while these entries report median perplexity rather than a capability measure. Other task results do not measure refusal.

untested.parts: All-layer, all-position projection ablation of the DiffMean direction; adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; general capability under the refusal intervention (the MMLU/GSM8K results are for generic λ=−3 steering, not refusal).
Separate encoding of harmfulness and refusal; this is argued but not measured.

record.verdict_notes: Refusal is a side experiment in a steering-method paper, and the CAA rows are baselines for the authors' method. The CAA refusal vector's layer (20, unlike the main-text CAA layers 29–31), token positions and norm are not specified, so λ values cannot be compared with the original's ablation. N=100 with keyword scoring and no uncertainty reported. E4's PPL of 30.4 vs 13.4 suggests a fluency cost at the only CAA setting that moved refusal.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not ablate the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction at every layer and position, add that direction on harmless requests, or test general capability under the refusal-specific intervention.
Whether jailbreak attacks suppress the claimed direction, or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is better described by an affine space, cone, or dominant direction plus others.
Whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from the refusal decision.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
How refusal training choices determine whether a removable direction exists.

rows.operation_detail: Multi-layer decision-point SAE-circuit steering with λ = −3
rows.note: This is a multi-layer SAE-circuit intervention, not ablation of the claimed difference-in-means direction.
rows.check: Multi-layer SAE decision-point circuit (the study's own method), not the harmful-minus-harmless DiffMean direction, so it cannot show V1's effect. The 0% refusal also comes with median PPL 35.7 vs 13.4 base.

rows.note: This is a multi-layer SAE-circuit intervention, not ablation of the claimed direction.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Single-layer CAA steering at layer 20 with λ = −5
rows.note: CAA is described as using an input-level harmful-versus-benign DiffMean vector; this coefficient is not the same as the claim's all-layer, all-position ablation.
rows.check: Single-layer (layer 20) activation subtraction, not ablation. The vector norm and extraction positions are not stated, so λ is not comparable to the original. Median PPL rises to 30.4 from 13.4.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Single-layer CAA steering at layer 20 with λ = −3
rows.note: The authors describe CAA at the identical coefficient as leaving refusal virtually intact.
rows.check: Single-layer subtraction at λ=−3 gives 92% vs 89% base; the authors call refusal 'virtually intact'. This is not directional ablation.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Single-layer CAA steering at layer 20 with λ = −1
rows.note: CAA is described as an input-level harmful-versus-benign DiffMean method.
rows.check: A 5-point drop (84% vs 89%) on 100 prompts with keyword scoring. It is a small move within likely noise, and the intervention is single-layer subtraction, not ablation.

relationships.condition: Single-layer (layer 20) subtraction of the harmful-vs-benign DiffMean vector on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, AdvBench, λ∈{−1,−3,−5}
relationships.reason: Refusal stays at 84–92% at λ=−1/−3 and only falls to 69% at λ=−5, with a PPL rise (E1, E4, E5, E6). Single-layer addition-style use of the direction does not remove refusal, though full ablation was not tested.
relationships.display_finding: Refusal remained 84–92% at λ=−1 or −3 and fell only to 69% at λ=−5, with increased perplexity.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Single-layer input-level CAA on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, AdvBench
reader_labels.reason: At λ = −3, refusal remains at 92% versus 89% unsteered, which the authors call virtually intact; this limits the claim for this CAA setting but is not the claimed all-layer ablation (E1, E5).
